title: Beware of assessing prerequisite knowledge in your retrieval Do Now
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton argues that a Do Now mixing unrelated retrieval questions with prerequisite-knowledge questions causes trouble. Drawing on a school visit where a quadratic-factorising prerequisite question stretched a planned 10-minute Do Now to 18 minutes, he shows how the mixed format wrecks timing, invites copying and makes routines hard to automate. His move is to separate the two jobs: keep the Do Now as four unrelated retrieval questions, then run a distinct, snappy prerequisite check one question at a time on mini-whiteboards or diagnostic multiple-choice. The post is a practical lesson-structure argument for maths teachers.
points: A prerequisite question cannot be abandoned when students struggle, so it breaks the 'move on and return later' logic that keeps a retrieval Do Now to time.
Longer individual work on a question gives students a chance to glimpse a neighbour's answer, which corrupts exactly the check that most needs to be reliable.
One prerequisite question rarely covers the several foundations a new concept rests on, so mixed Do Nows under-test.
A separate, labelled prerequisite phase can flex between 30 seconds and 15 minutes without disturbing the Do Now routine.
quotes: Many teachers and departments like to have their Do Now boxed off in around 10 minutes. This is only possible if you can move on from a question if students are still struggling. Such a move is only possible if the question has nothing to do with the rest of the lesson, as you know you can return to it at a later date. It is not possible to do so if the question assesses prerequisite knowledge.

Even though the Do Now was conducted in silence, and the teacher reinforced the importance of independent work, it is all too easy to catch a glimpse of your partner’s answer to a question when you are working for more than 5 minutes. And, having seen that answer, it is all too easy to change your answer, convincing yourself you knew it all along. This, of course, reduces the reliability of the subsequent check for understanding.
Most new concepts need to be built upon the solid foundations of several existing concepts. Hence, to assess the strength of these foundations, you usually require several questions.
I am a huge fan of routines, for both teachers and students. And especially at the start of lessons. But mixed Do Nows like the one above make routines so much harder to establish and automate.
No, I favour a four-question Do Now, where each question is designed to strengthen the memory of content unrelated to the rest of the lesson, delivered something like this.

However, following that, I like a section of the lesson dedicated to assessing prerequisite knowledge. This works best one question at a time to reduce instances of copying and keep up a hearty pace, eliciting mass participation by either asking students to respond on mini-whiteboards or by using multiple-choice diagnostic questions and ABCD cards.
